core: The distinction between evidence (what the sources show) and interpretation (the argument built to explain it)
Why a good historical interpretation is not merely an opinion: it is supported by evidence and reasoning and can be tested against the sources
Corroboration: checking a claim against multiple independent sources, and why independence matters
Why reasonable historians can still disagree (incomplete evidence, weighing sources differently, asking different questions)
How to tell a stronger interpretation from a weaker one (fit, corroboration, addressing counter-evidence, not over-reaching)
supporting: History as argument/interpretation/consequence rather than a fixed list of facts
Historical inference as reasoning from a body of evidence
outOfScope: Full treatment of primary vs secondary sources (reference only; owned by :primary-sources and :secondary-sources)
Bias and perspective as a standalone topic (:bias-and-perspective)
Causation as a specific kind of interpretation (:causation)

claims.claim: History is fundamentally about argument, interpretation, and consequence; doing it well means using appropriate evidence, assessing it properly, and drawing meaningful conclusions from it.
Evidence is what surviving sources show and can be re-checked in the source; interpretation is the argument that explains the evidence and goes beyond any single source.
Analyzing a primary source involves observing details, then generating and testing hypotheses about it, then asking further questions, an evidence-to-inference loop.

Corroboration means comparing details across multiple sources to determine consistency; it is one of four historical reading skills (with sourcing, contextualization, close reading) in the SHEG framework associated with Sam Wineburg.

A single partisan source can be genuine evidence of the attitudes of its creators while its factual claims about opponents cannot be accepted as fact; some claims are not historical facts because they are not agreed upon and verifiable from multiple points of view.
Historical conclusions are tentative and impermanent; new evidence and perspectives can alter the understanding of the past, so historians link new arguments to prior scholarship.
Edward Gibbon's History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire was published in six volumes between 1776 and 1788 and emphasized the rise of Christianity as a cause of Rome's decline.

Later historians have substantially reassessed Gibbon's Christianity-centered thesis, emphasizing multiple factors (fiscal strain, leadership, epidemics, external pressure) and noting the Christian Eastern Roman Empire survived for centuries, so Christianity alone cannot explain the West's collapse.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What caused the decline of the Western Roman Empire.
positions: Gibbon (1776-1788) emphasized the rise of Christianity as a central cause.
Modern historians emphasize multiple corroborated factors and, in the 'late antiquity' tradition, reframe the period as transformation rather than simple collapse.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Used in the lesson as an illustration that reasonable historians disagree when they weigh incomplete evidence differently and ask different questions; the survival of the Christian East is presented as counter-evidence against a single-cause thesis. The lesson does not declare a single correct cause.
